clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Gastroenteritis with orthostatic dehydration evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Gastroenteritis with orthostatic dehydration is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Acute Gastroenteritis with mild orthostatic dehydration, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Gastroenteritis with orthostatic dehydration.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Bacterial gastroenteritis (Vibrio, Salmonella given seafood exposure) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Bloody diarrhea or high fever — suggests invasive bacterial infection needing different management.
management_principles: Check orthostatic vitals and skin turgor to assess for Acute Gastroenteritis with mild orthostatic dehydration
Administer IV fluid bolus, oral rehydration, and antiemetic (Ondansetron)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Acute Gastroenteritis with mild orthostatic dehydration. acute watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and mild fever after buffet eating. 32M presents with 12 hours of watery diarrhea (8 episodes), diffuse abdominal cramping, and a low-grade fever of 37.8C. Reports eating at a seafood buffet yesterday. Feels dizzy when standing up.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Acute Gastroenteritis with mild orthostatic dehydration.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Acute Gastroenteritis with mild orthostatic dehydration.
reference_soap.plan: Check orthostatic vitals and skin turgor to assess dehydration severity. Administer an IV fluid bolus, oral rehydration, and an antiemetic (ondansetron). Discuss the typically self-limiting course, and avoid loperamide if a bacterial cause (e.g., Vibrio, Salmonella) is suspected given the seafood exposure. Refer to a specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling if symptoms persist or worsen.

teaching.one_liner: A foodborne infection causing watery diarrhea and cramping, with significant fluid loss producing lightheadedness on standing — managed with fluids and antiemetics rather than antidiarrheals if a bacterial cause is suspected.
differentials: Bacterial gastroenteritis (Vibrio, Salmonella given seafood exposure)
red_flags: Bloody diarrhea or high fever — suggests invasive bacterial infection needing different management

must_ask.say: How many watery stools have you had, and is there any blood?
What did you eat at the buffet, especially any seafood?
Do you feel dizzy when you stand up?
Have you been able to keep fluids down?

history.answer: I've had severe watery diarrhea and bad belly cramps since early this morning after eating at a seafood buffet yesterday.
It started suddenly about 12 hours ago, around 4 in the morning.
I've gone about 8 times today, and it's completely liquid and watery, not oily or greasy.
No, I haven't seen any blood or mucus in my stool.
Yes, the stomach cramps and diarrhea actually woke me up from my sleep in the middle of the night.
The cramps are all over my stomach and ease up a little right after I use the bathroom, but I don't feel like I constantly need to strain.
I felt hot and measured my temperature at 37.8 degrees Celsius this morning, but I haven't had shaking chills.
I've been feeling quite nauseous all morning, but I haven't actually vomited.
Whenever I stand up, I feel very dizzy and lightheaded, like I might pass out.
My mouth feels completely parched and sticky, and I feel thirsty all the time.
I've only managed to pee once since this morning, and it was a tiny amount that looked dark yellow.
I've tried sipping water, but my stomach is so unsettled that it's tough to drink much.
I ate raw shrimp and oysters at a seafood buffet with a coworker yesterday evening, but I'm not sure if he got sick too.
No, I haven't traveled anywhere recently, haven't been camping, and only drink tap or bottled water.
No, I haven't taken any antibiotics lately, haven't been hospitalized, and haven't started any new medications.
No, my weight has been completely stable.
No, I've never had any trouble digesting milk, dairy, or wheat products.
No, I usually have one normal bowel movement a day, and this isn't caused by stress.
No, I don't have any joint pain, skin rashes, mouth sores, or eye redness.
No, I haven't felt a racing heart at rest, no heat intolerance, and no facial flushing.
I think I have severe food poisoning from the seafood, or maybe I'm badly dehydrated.
I'm really worried that I'll need IV fluid drips or have to stay in the hospital.
I'm hoping to get some medicine to stop the diarrhea and some fluids so I can recover quickly.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I've never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or vitamins.
No, I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only have one or two beers occasionally with friends, but I haven't had any alcohol in the past week.
I work as an office clerk and live in an apartment with a roommate.
No one in my family has chronic bowel diseases, inflammatory bowel disease, or colon cancer.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 37.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Blood pressure drops from 110/70 mmHg supine to 96/60 mmHg standing, while heart rate rises from 98 to 118 beats per minute with symptomatic lightheadedness.
Patient appears fatigued and mildly pale, lying supine on the bed in mild distress from abdominal cramping.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are clear and anicteric.
Oral mucous membranes and tongue appear visibly dry and sticky without pharyngeal exudate.
Decreased skin turgor with slow recoil, and peripheral capillary refill is delayed at 3 seconds.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without distension, visible peristalsis, or surgical scars.
Hyperactive, frequent, high-pitched bowel sounds heard throughout all four quadrants.
Diffusely tympanitic throughout without shifting dullness or fluid wave.
Mild, diffuse tenderness on palpation across all quadrants without involuntary guarding or abdominal wall rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited in any abdominal quadrant.
Negative tenderness at McBurney's point, and negative Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs.
Normal perianal skin and sphincter tone; empty rectal vault with watery brown residue, negative for gross blood.
